claim: Insect wings are a key innovation that contributed to the explosive diversification of insects.
source: Insect wings, a key innovation that contributed to the explosive diversification of insects, are recognized for their remarkable variation and many splendid adaptations.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary significance of insect wings, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Classical morphological work subdivides insect wings into several distinct domains along the anteroposterior (AP) axis.
source: Classical morphological work subdivides insect wings into several distinct domains along the anteroposterior (AP) axis, each of which can evolve relatively independently to produce the myriad forms we see in nature.
evidence: This refers to established morphological work in the field, representing scientific knowledge.

claim: Each AP domain of insect wings can evolve relatively independently to produce diverse forms.
source: Classical morphological work subdivides insect wings into several distinct domains along the anteroposterior (AP) axis, each of which can evolve relatively independently to produce the myriad forms we see in nature.
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary independence of wing domains, based on established knowledge.

claim: The transcription factor mirror acts as a selector gene to differentiate a far posterior domain in the butterfly wing.
source: Here, we show that the transcription factor mirror acts as a selector gene to differentiate a far posterior domain in the butterfly wing, classically defined as the vannus, and has effects on wing shape, scale morphology, and color pattern.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including expression analysis and CRISPR knockouts.

claim: The far posterior domain differentiated by mirror is classically defined as the vannus.
source: Here, we show that the transcription factor mirror acts as a selector gene to differentiate a far posterior domain in the butterfly wing, classically defined as the vannus, and has effects on wing shape, scale morphology, and color pattern.
evidence: This connects the molecular finding to classical anatomical terminology.

claim: mirror has effects on wing shape, scale morphology, and color pattern.
source: Here, we show that the transcription factor mirror acts as a selector gene to differentiate a far posterior domain in the butterfly wing, classically defined as the vannus, and has effects on wing shape, scale morphology, and color pattern.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental knockout data showing multiple phenotypic effects.

claim: The D. melanogaster wing blade has been reduced to represent only a portion of the archetypal insect wing.
source: Our results support models of how selector genes may facilitate evolutionarily individuation of distinct AP domains in insect wings outside of Drosophila and suggest that the D. melanogaster wing blade has been reduced to represent only a portion of the archetypal insect wing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of mirror function in butterflies versus Drosophila.

claim: The diversity of lepidopteran color patterns follows relatively simple rules involving an evolutionarily conserved set of spot and stripe pattern elements.
source: Interestingly, the diversity of lepidopteran color patterns appears to follow relatively simple rules, wherein an evolutionarily conserved set of spot and stripe pattern elements can vary in size, color, and presence/absence along the anteroposterior (AP) axis (Nijhout, 1991; Nijhout, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nijhout's work.

claim: Butterfly wings can be subdivided into five AP domains, bounded by the M1, M3, Cu2, and 2A veins.
source: Surveys of wing pattern diversity across butterflies, considering both natural variation and genetic mutants, suggest that wings can be subdivided into five AP domains, bounded by the M1, M3, Cu2, and 2A veins as summarized in Figure 1A (McKenna et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McKenna et al., 2020 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Within each AP domain, there is a strong correlation between pattern variation and wing morphology.
source: Within each domain, there is a strong correlation between pattern variation and wing morphology, and, conversely, between domains, there is a relative degree of independence in morphological variation.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between pattern and morphology within domains.

claim: Between AP domains, there is a relative degree of independence in morphological variation.
source: Within each domain, there is a strong correlation between pattern variation and wing morphology, and, conversely, between domains, there is a relative degree of independence in morphological variation.
evidence: This is an observation about the independence of variation between domains.

claim: The transcription factors engrailed and spalt define AP domains in developing Drosophila melanogaster wings.
source: The transcription factors engrailed and spalt define AP domains in developing fly wings (Guillén et al., 1995; de Celis et al., 1996; Morata and Lawrence, 1975) and exhibit expression patterns in butterflies that suggest some functions may be conserved.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to work in Drosophila.

claim: engrailed and spalt exhibit expression patterns in butterflies that suggest some functions may be conserved.
source: The transcription factors engrailed and spalt define AP domains in developing fly wings (Guillén et al., 1995; de Celis et al., 1996; Morata and Lawrence, 1975) and exhibit expression patterns in butterflies that suggest some functions may be conserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on expression pattern observations.

claim: In butterflies, engrailed transcription occurs across the entire region posterior to the M1 vein.
source: In butterflies, engrailed transcription occurs across the entire region posterior to the M1 vein, while its paralog invected marks a largely overlapping region between M1 and 2A (Carroll et al., 1994; Keys et al., 1999; Banerjee and Monteiro, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of engrailed expression in butterflies.

claim: invected marks a largely overlapping region between M1 and 2A in butterflies.
source: In butterflies, engrailed transcription occurs across the entire region posterior to the M1 vein, while its paralog invected marks a largely overlapping region between M1 and 2A (Carroll et al., 1994; Keys et al., 1999; Banerjee and Monteiro, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of invected expression in butterflies.

claim: spalt expression in butterflies consistently marks a region between the R2 and M3 veins.
source: spalt expression is more dynamic and complex in butterflies, but appears to consistently mark a region between the R2 and M3 veins (Banerjee and Monteiro, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banerjee and Monteiro, 2020.

claim: mirror was identified as a potential candidate selector gene based on previous mRNA-seq studies.
source: We initially identified the transcription factor mirror as a potential candidate selector gene based on previous mRNA-seq studies (Hanly et al., 2019), coupled with D. melanogaster work showing that mirror specifies the alula – a small membranous lobe at the posterior base of the wing in some dipterans (Figure 1C and D; Kehl et al., 1998; Foronda et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanly et al., 2019.

claim: In D. melanogaster, mirror specifies the alula, a small membranous lobe at the posterior base of the wing.
source: We initially identified the transcription factor mirror as a potential candidate selector gene based on previous mRNA-seq studies (Hanly et al., 2019), coupled with D. melanogaster work showing that mirror specifies the alula – a small membranous lobe at the posterior base of the wing in some dipterans (Figure 1C and D; Kehl et al., 1998; Foronda et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kehl et al., 1998 and Foronda et al., 2009, and illustrated in Figure 1C and D.

claim: mirror is expressed throughout the wing domain posterior to the 2A vein boundary in Junonia coenia last-instar imaginal discs.
source: We used in situ hybridization to visualize mirror mRNA localization in the last-instar imaginal discs of the common buckeye butterfly, Junonia coenia, and observed mirror expression throughout the wing domain posterior to the 2A vein boundary (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: mirror expression precisely marks the vannus, or anal region, of the butterfly wing.
source: This expression precisely marks the vannus, or anal region (Figure 1B and E), of the butterfly wing – a distinct posterior domain of the wing blade populated by the anal (A) veins and bordered anteriorly by the claval fold between the cubital (Cu) and A veins in the hindwing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data and illustrated in Figures 1B, 1E, and 2B.

claim: The vannus is a distinct posterior domain of the wing blade populated by the anal (A) veins.
source: This expression precisely marks the vannus, or anal region (Figure 1B and E), of the butterfly wing – a distinct posterior domain of the wing blade populated by the anal (A) veins and bordered anteriorly by the claval fold between the cubital (Cu) and A veins in the hindwing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an anatomical description based on established knowledge and illustrated in figures.

claim: The vannus is bordered anteriorly by the claval fold between the cubital (Cu) and A veins in the hindwing.
source: This expression precisely marks the vannus, or anal region (Figure 1B and E), of the butterfly wing – a distinct posterior domain of the wing blade populated by the anal (A) veins and bordered anteriorly by the claval fold between the cubital (Cu) and A veins in the hindwing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an anatomical description illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The color patterns defining the wing blade terminate at the 2A vein in various butterfly species.
source: As observed in various representative species across different butterfly families, this region of the hindwing is distinct from the rest of the wing; the color patterns defining the wing blade terminate at the 2A vein, and in many species, it is marked by scales that differ in morphology and lack color patterns found in anterior regions of the wing (Figures 1B and 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an observation supported by images in Figures 1B, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In many butterfly species, the vannus is marked by scales that differ in morphology and lack color patterns found in anterior regions of the wing.
source: As observed in various representative species across different butterfly families, this region of the hindwing is distinct from the rest of the wing; the color patterns defining the wing blade terminate at the 2A vein, and in many species, it is marked by scales that differ in morphology and lack color patterns found in anterior regions of the wing (Figures 1B and 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an observation supported by images in Figures 1B, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The vannus has been proposed to represent the posterior-most color pattern domain in butterflies.
source: This region has been proposed to represent the posterior-most color pattern domain in butterflies (Figures 1A and 2B; McKenna et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McKenna et al., 2020 and illustrated in Figures 1A and 2B.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 mosaic knockouts of mirror in J. coenia consistently exhibited distinctive phenotypes only in the mirror-expressing posterior vannus region.
source: To functionally assess the role of mirror in wing development, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 mosaic knockouts (mKOs) targeting the coding region of J. coenia mirror. We recovered many mKO mutants that consistently exhibited several distinctive phenotypes (Figure 2C, D, and F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Figure 2—figure supplement 4), but only ever in the mirror-expressing posterior vannus region:
evidence: This is supported by experimental CRISPR knockout data shown in multiple figures.

claim: mirror knockouts affect multiple aspects of wing morphology, including scale shape and coloration, overall wing shape, and wing venation.
source: Second, mirror knockouts appear to affect multiple aspects of wing morphology, including scale shape and coloration, overall wing shape, and wing venation.
evidence: This is an observation from the knockout experiments shown in the figures.

claim: The loss of mirror function resulted in transformation, not loss, of the posterior domain.
source: Finally, the loss of mirror function resulted in transformation, not loss, of the posterior domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the knockout phenotypes observed in the experiments.

claim: In mirror mKO individuals, the mirror-expressing cells posterior to the 2A vein were not simply lost but changed in identity.
source: Even in mKO individuals that appeared to have a mutant phenotype across the entire posterior region, the mirror-expressing cells posterior to the 2A vein were not simply lost – the wing field continues well past the 2A vein. Instead, the identities of the post-2A scale cells changed in color and structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the knockout experiments.

claim: The expansion of multiple color pattern systems into the posterior domain of mutants was observed in mirror knockouts.
source: In this respect, the expansion of multiple color pattern systems into the posterior domain of mutants was particularly compelling because the loss of central symmetry system and submarginal patterns in the post-2A vannus region is commonly observed in Lepidoptera (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the knockout experiments, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The loss of central symmetry system and submarginal patterns in the post-2A vannus region is commonly observed in Lepidoptera.
source: In this respect, the expansion of multiple color pattern systems into the posterior domain of mutants was particularly compelling because the loss of central symmetry system and submarginal patterns in the post-2A vannus region is commonly observed in Lepidoptera (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lepidopteran wing patterns, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The patterning information for color pattern elements may occur in a latent form that is masked by mirror effects.
source: The ability to reconstitute these complex color pattern elements in the posterior domain by knocking out a single transcription factor leads us to speculate that their patterning information may occur in a latent form that is masked by mirror effects.
evidence: This is speculation based on the knockout phenotypes observed.

claim: mirror acts as a selector gene necessary to define the identity of the far posterior wing domain.
source: Together, our expression and knockout data suggest that mirror acts as a selector gene necessary to define the identity of the far posterior wing domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression and knockout data.

claim: mirror provides a molecular explanation for how different AP domains of the butterfly wing may be individuated to independently evolve their own shape and color pattern variations.
source: First, it provides a molecular explanation for how different AP domains of the butterfly wing may be individuated to independently evolve their own shape and color pattern variations.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: Previous authors have proposed the existence of individuated domains in butterfly wings and speculated that they may be specified by selector genes.
source: Previous authors have proposed the existence of such individuated domains and speculated that they may be specified by selector genes (McKenna et al., 2020; Abbasi and Marcus, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McKenna et al., 2020 and Abbasi and Marcus, 2017.

claim: The role of mirror in specifying the vannus provides a link between molecular developmental biology and Snodgrass' classical anatomical designations of the insect wing fields.
source: Next, the role of mirror in specifying the vannus provides an important link between molecular developmental biology and Snodgrass' classical anatomical designations of the insect wing fields – i.e., the remigium, the vannus, and the jugum (Figure 1E; Snodgrass, 1935).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the molecular findings to classical anatomy, with citation to Snodgrass, 1935.

claim: Snodgrass' classical anatomical designations of the insect wing fields include the remigium, the vannus, and the jugum.
source: Next, the role of mirror in specifying the vannus provides an important link between molecular developmental biology and Snodgrass' classical anatomical designations of the insect wing fields – i.e., the remigium, the vannus, and the jugum (Figure 1E; Snodgrass, 1935).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge from Snodgrass, 1935, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: The remigium and the vannus are dominant features of most insect wings.
source: The remigium and the vannus are dominant features of most insect wings, while the jugum is a smaller lobe-like feature that is reduced or lost in many clades.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about insect wings.

claim: The jugum is a smaller lobe-like feature that is reduced or lost in many insect clades.
source: The remigium and the vannus are dominant features of most insect wings, while the jugum is a smaller lobe-like feature that is reduced or lost in many clades.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about insect wings.

claim: The remigium is the major anterior wing blade that is directly articulated by thoracic motor musculature to power flight.
source: The remigium is the major anterior wing blade that is directly articulated by thoracic motor musculature to power flight and is typically divided from the vannus by a distinct wing fold (e.g. the 'anal fold' in butterflies).
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge about insect wings.

claim: The remigium is typically divided from the vannus by a distinct wing fold.
source: The remigium is the major anterior wing blade that is directly articulated by thoracic motor musculature to power flight and is typically divided from the vannus by a distinct wing fold (e.g. the 'anal fold' in butterflies).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about insect wings.

claim: In many insect orders, the vannus is a prominent fan-like structure.
source: In many insect orders, the vannus is a prominent fan-like structure, which can be a greatly enlarged gliding surface in some hemimetabolous clades such as Orthoptera (crickets and grasshoppers), Dictyoptera (mantids and roaches), Phasmatodea (stick insects), and Plecoptera (stoneflies).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about insect wings across different orders.

claim: The vannus can be a greatly enlarged gliding surface in some hemimetabolous clades such as Orthoptera, Dictyoptera, Phasmatodea, and Plecoptera.
source: In many insect orders, the vannus is a prominent fan-like structure, which can be a greatly enlarged gliding surface in some hemimetabolous clades such as Orthoptera (crickets and grasshoppers), Dictyoptera (mantids and roaches), Phasmatodea (stick insects), and Plecoptera (stoneflies).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about insect wings in specific orders.

claim: mirror knockdown in the hemimetabolous milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus causes developmental defects in the claval and anal furrows in the posterior wing.
source: Importantly, mirror knockdown in the hemimetabolous milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus causes developmental defects in the claval and anal furrows in the posterior wing (Fisher et al., 2021), which leads us to infer that mirror's role in determining the vannus may be deeply conserved in insects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2021.

claim: mirror's role in determining the vannus may be deeply conserved in insects.
source: Importantly, mirror knockdown in the hemimetabolous milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus causes developmental defects in the claval and anal furrows in the posterior wing (Fisher et al., 2021), which leads us to infer that mirror's role in determining the vannus may be deeply conserved in insects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Oncopeltus data cited from Fisher et al., 2021.

claim: The developmental individuation of the posterior domain by mirror may have facilitated the remarkable diversification of the vannus across the insects.
source: This prompts us to speculate that the developmental individuation of the posterior domain by mirror facilitated the remarkable diversification of the vannus across the insects.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary significance of mirror's role.

claim: The alula in D. melanogaster may represent an evolutionarily reduced vannus.
source: Finally, the function of mirror in determining the alula in D. melanogaster (Kehl et al., 1998) suggests that the alula may represent an evolutionarily reduced vannus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mirror function in Drosophila and butterflies, with citation to Kehl et al., 1998.

claim: The D. melanogaster wing blade is a lone remigium, representing only one-third of the archetypal insect wing.
source: The ramifications of this are significant for reconstructing the history of the insect wing, because they suggest that the D. melanogaster wing blade is a lone remigium – only one-third of the archetypal insect wing (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of Drosophila wing structure to the archetypal insect wing, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: The dipteran jugum appears to have been lost entirely, except perhaps as a membranous haltere cover (calypter) in the Calyptratae clade.
source: The dipteran jugum appears to have been lost entirely, except perhaps as a membranous haltere cover (calypter) in the Calyptratae clade, as speculated by Snodgrass, 1935.
evidence: This is speculation attributed to Snodgrass, 1935.

claim: A more comprehensive understanding of the development and evolution of insect wings requires work in species that have wings more representative of the complete ancestral blueprint.
source: Thus, while flies have been an important model for characterizing genes and processes that build insect wings, a more comprehensive understanding of the development and evolution of insect wings requires work in species that have wings more representative of the complete ancestral blueprint.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of Drosophila as a model and the need for broader comparative studies.

claim: Mutant phenotypes in mirror knockouts were never observed anterior to the 2A vein.
source: First, across all mKO replicates, we never observed mutant phenotypes anterior to the 2A vein, which suggests that mirror effects are limited to the far posterior domain in which we observed mirror expression.
evidence: This is an observation from the knockout experiments.

claim: mirror effects are limited to the far posterior domain in which mirror expression was observed.
source: First, across all mKO replicates, we never observed mutant phenotypes anterior to the 2A vein, which suggests that mirror effects are limited to the far posterior domain in which we observed mirror expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial restriction of knockout phenotypes.

claim: The 2A vein marks a clear posterior color pattern boundary across multiple butterfly families.
source: (B) Examples of the 2A vein marking a clear posterior color pattern boundary across multiple butterfly families.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with examples from multiple butterfly families.

claim: The calypters are only found in the Calyptratae clade of Diptera.
source: (C) Proximal posterior features of the archetypal dipteran wing include the calypters, which are only found in the Calyptratae clade, and the alula, a lobe at the base of the wing blade (McAlpine et al., 1981).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from McAlpine et al., 1981 and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: mirror RNAi knockdowns result in highly specific loss of the alula in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: (D) mirror RNAi knockdowns result in highly specific loss of the alula in Drosophila melanogaster (Kehl et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kehl et al., 1998 and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Homologies of the remigium, vannus, and jugum domains with features of the dipteran wing or butterfly wing pattern boundaries have remained unclear.
source: (E) Snodgrass' model of the archetypal insect wing specifies three major domains along the anteroposterior axis: the remigium, the vannus, and the jugum. Homologies of these domains with the features of the dipteran wing (C), or butterfly wing pattern boundaries (A), have remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge regarding homologies, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: In J. coenia, mirror is expressed posterior to the 2A vein in the late last-instar hindwing imaginal discs.
source: (A) In J. coenia, mirror (red) is expressed posterior to the 2A vein in the late last-instar hindwing imaginal discs, marking the region that will develop into the vannus.
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2A.

claim: In adult J. coenia butterfly wings, the vannus is a posterior lobe with silvery scales devoid of color patterns found anterior to 2A.
source: (B) In adult butterfly wings, the vannus is the wing field posterior to the 2A vein, shown here in J. coenia as a posterior lobe with silvery scales devoid of color patterns found anterior to 2A.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Targeted mosaic knockouts of mirror result in loss of vannus features in J. coenia.
source: (C) Targeted mosaic knockouts (mKOs) of mirror result in loss of vannus features in J. coenia.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mirror mKO phenotypes include loss of posterior lobe, loss of 3A vein, ectopic branching of 2A vein, and posterior extension of color patterns.
source: (E) Annotation of full effect mutant phenotype in the opposing wing from the individual in (D) highlights loss of lobe, loss of 3A, ectopic branching of 2A, and posterior extension of color patterns.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Partial mirror mKOs show transformation of posterior lobe and extension of color patterns that terminate at the mutant clonal boundary.
source: (F) Annotation of a partial mKO highlights transformation of posterior lobe and extension of color patterns, both of which terminate at the mutant clonal boundary.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In partial mirror mKOs, ectopic branching of 2A occurs in the mutant region while 3A is preserved in the wild-type region.
source: (G) The individual shown in (F) also shows ectopic branching of 2A in the mutant region, but preservation of 3A in the wild-type region.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G.

claim: mirror is expressed posterior to the 2A vein in last-instar forewing imaginal discs of J. coenia.
source: (A) mirror is expressed posterior to the 2A vein in last-instar forewing imaginal discs of J. coenia.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of wingless observed by HCR precisely matches expression in wing margin peripheral tissue and discal bands as previously described from chromogenic in situ.
source: (B) Double in situ of mirror (Channel 1: 647 nm) and wingless (Channel 2: 546 nm) in last instar J. coenia hindwing imaginal discs. Expression of wingless observed by HCR precisely matches expression in wing margin peripheral tissue and discal bands (white arrow) as previously described from chromogenic in situ (de Celis et al., 1996), thus providing a positive control for our HCR protocol.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and supported by citation to de Celis et al., 1996.

claim: mirror mKOs result in complete or partial transformation of the vannus.
source: (A) Comparison of wild-type dorsal hindwing to mutant wings reveals complete or partial transformation of the vannus (black arrows), expansion of color patterns into the posterior wing margin (white arrows) along with vein aberrations (denoted by *), or total loss (denoted by -).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mirror mKOs result in expansion of color patterns into the posterior wing margin.
source: (A) Comparison of wild-type dorsal hindwing to mutant wings reveals complete or partial transformation of the vannus (black arrows), expansion of color patterns into the posterior wing margin (white arrows) along with vein aberrations (denoted by *), or total loss (denoted by -).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mirror mKOs result in vein aberrations or total loss of veins.
source: (A) Comparison of wild-type dorsal hindwing to mutant wings reveals complete or partial transformation of the vannus (black arrows), expansion of color patterns into the posterior wing margin (white arrows) along with vein aberrations (denoted by *), or total loss (denoted by -).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Contralateral hindwing pairs from the same individuals show asymmetry in clonal mutations affecting posterior wing margin phenotype.
source: The bottom panels show contralateral hindwing pairs from the same individuals showing asymmetry in clonal mutations affecting posterior wing margin phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mirror mKOs in ventral J. coenia hindwings result in the expansion of color pattern elements.
source: Related to Figure 2B–E. mirror mKOs in ventral J. coenia hindwings resulting in the expansion of color pattern elements (white arrows) as seen in asymmetric contralateral pairs from the same mutant individuals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: mKOs of mirror result in anomalies along the forewing 2A vein, including vein bifurcation and ectopic vein fragments.
source: mKOs of mirror result in anomalies along the forewing 2A vein, including vein bifurcation and ectopic vein fragments, which are often associated with color pattern disruption.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Forewing 2A vein anomalies in mirror mKOs are often associated with color pattern disruption.
source: mKOs of mirror result in anomalies along the forewing 2A vein, including vein bifurcation and ectopic vein fragments, which are often associated with color pattern disruption.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A reciprocal BLAST was performed to identify orthologs of D. melanogaster Iroquois Complex genes in J. coenia and other species.
source: We performed a reciprocal BLAST of amino acid sequences of D. melanogaster Iroquois Complex genes araucan, caupolican, and mirror to identify their orthologs in the latest J. coenia and Heliconius erato lativitta genome sequences on lepbase.org and Tribolium castaneum and Apis mellifera on NCBI.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatic method used.

claim: Two sgRNAs targeting the homeobox domain of mirror were used for CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis in J. coenia.
source: Two single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs; sgRNA1-5'-GAATGGACTTGAACGGGGCA; sgRNA2-5'-AGAAACAGGGTCGATGATGA) targeting the homeobox domain of mirror were mixed with 500 ng/μL of Cas9 nuclease and injected to J. coenia eggs 0.5–4 hr after oviposition (n=1042 eggs) as previously described (Zhang and Reed, 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, with citation to Zhang and Reed, 2017.

claim: 1042 J. coenia eggs were injected with CRISPR-Cas9 reagents targeting mirror.
source: Two single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs; sgRNA1-5'-GAATGGACTTGAACGGGGCA; sgRNA2-5'-AGAAACAGGGTCGATGATGA) targeting the homeobox domain of mirror were mixed with 500 ng/μL of Cas9 nuclease and injected to J. coenia eggs 0.5–4 hr after oviposition (n=1042 eggs) as previously described (Zhang and Reed, 2017).
evidence: This is experimental data about the number of eggs injected.

claim: 99 G0 adults survived from the CRISPR injection experiment.
source: Wings of surviving G0 adults (n=99) were assayed for anomalies to detect mKO phenotypes (n=29).
evidence: This is experimental data about survival rate.

claim: 29 individuals showed mKO phenotypes out of 99 surviving G0 adults.
source: Wings of surviving G0 adults (n=99) were assayed for anomalies to detect mKO phenotypes (n=29).
evidence: This is experimental data about the frequency of mutant phenotypes.
